text: {"lesson":{"schemaVersion":1,"title":"Lesson 19: The Lightning Thief and Myths, Academic Discussion","lessonType":"academic-discussion","header":{"focusStandards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"],"supportingStandards":["SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"],"eldStandards":["ELD.PI.6.1","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PII.6.1"],"mediaLiteracyStandards":[],"objectives":[{"kind":"content","text":"Students will synthesize what they have read in Chapters 1–12 of The Lightning Thief and in traditional myths from Investigation 1 to discuss how the novel's mythic elements reflect cultural values, fears, and recurring patterns."},{"kind":"language","text":"Students will use evidence-based discussion stems, comparison language (e.g., similarly, in contrast, both stories), and formal English to pose and answer questions, paraphrase peers, and cite specific scenes, characters, and events."},{"kind":"foundational-skills","text":"Students will come to the discussion prepared with marked evidence, follow group roles and norms, and speak at an appropriate volume and pace in formal English so peers can follow their reasoning."}],"essentialQuestions":["How do myths reflect cultural values?"],"connections":{"knowledgeBuilding":"Students have read Chapters 1–12 of The Lightning Thief and several traditional myths in Investigation 1. Today they pull those readings together to see which fears, values, and patterns keep appearing in the novel and in the myths.","enduringUnderstanding":"Myths are more than adventure stories. The monsters, heroes, gods, and conflicts in them show what a culture fears, respects, and wants to teach.","futureLessons":"The ideas students gather today feed the Meaning-Making Huddle (Flex Day) and bridge into Investigation 2. There they will keep asking how retellings of myths change across cultures and generations.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students must discuss and write about an essential question using evidence from several texts. Today they practice that skill by speaking with cited evidence from the novel and from myths."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"cultural value","definition":"an idea about what is important, right, or admirable to a group of people, such as courage, loyalty, or respect for nature","tier":"support"},{"word":"pattern","definition":"something that repeats in a story or across stories, such as a type of character, event, or conflict","tier":"support"},{"word":"synthesize","definition":"to combine ideas from more than one source to build a new understanding","tier":"support"},{"word":"paraphrase","definition":"to restate someone else's idea in your own words","tier":"support"},{"word":"formal English","definition":"the polished, respectful way of speaking used in school and professional settings, with complete sentences and precise words","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapters 1–12 (Ch. 11 pp. 178–187; Ch. 12 follows; Ch. 13 summary pp. 197–201 for homework)"},{"title":"Traditional myths from Investigation 1 (excerpts from other cultures)","pages":"Student copies from Investigation 1"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students warm up with a quick Turn and Talk that gets Chapter 12 and the essential question in mind.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Turn and Talk: Why Do Stories Look the Way They Do?","minutes":5,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.c"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Take out your copy of The Lightning Thief and your notes on Chapter 12. Turn to a partner and respond to the question you hear."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Percy's story is set in the modern world, but it is built from ancient Greek myths. Today we ask what those stories tell us about what people care about, then and now."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In Chapter 12, how do the characters treat nature, and what does the way they act suggest about what the author thinks people should value? Use one detail from the chapter."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"In Chapter 12, the characters notice damage to the natural world around them, and that makes it feel like a problem we have today. This suggests the author thinks people should care about the environment and think about how our actions affect it, even though the monsters and gods are from old myths."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Have students point to the exact scene in their books. Accept any text-grounded detail about nature or human actions in Chapter 12. If a pair cannot find one, send them back to their Chapter 12 annotations for two minutes. Invite two pairs to share."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today's discussion question is: How do myths reflect cultural values? You will use scenes from Chapters 1–12 and the myths we read in Investigation 1 to answer it."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students set group roles and norms, practice formal English discussion language, and begin a chart of patterns across the novel and myths.","activities":[{"id":"lab-norms-formal-english","title":"Roles, Norms, and Formal English","minutes":5,"standards":["SL.6.1.b","SL.6.6"],"routine":"Co-constructed norms","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Join your group of four. Choose roles: Facilitator, Evidence Tracker, Paraphraser, Connector. Help the class build discussion norms."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Each role has one job. The Facilitator makes sure everyone speaks and asks the next question. The Evidence Tracker says where evidence comes from, like the chapter or the myth title. The Paraphraser restates a classmate's idea before adding to it. The Connector links the novel to a myth."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Why do you think we speak in formal English during an academic discussion, and what does that sound like?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"We use formal English so everyone can understand our ideas and take them seriously. It sounds like complete sentences and precise words, like 'This scene suggests...' instead of 'It's kinda like...'. It also means a clear, steady voice."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Our norms: listen without interrupting, cite evidence by naming the chapter or myth, respond to ideas rather than people, and use formal English."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Post the four norms and the role names where all groups can see them. Remind students to switch to casual language when they are chatting but to use formal English when they speak to the group."}]},{"id":"lab-pattern-chart","title":"Start a Patterns Chart","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"On your chart, make three columns: Fears and Values, Scenes in The Lightning Thief (Chs. 1–12), Similar Moments in Myths from Other Cultures. Add at least two rows using your annotations."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A pattern is something that repeats. For example, gods may make human life hard, or heroes may face monsters that stand for something people fear. Watch for what repeats in the novel and in the myths."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one pattern you have noticed in the novel so far? Name the chapter or scene."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"One pattern is that Percy, a young hero, has to face a monster that is really dangerous, like the Minotaur or Medusa. In the Greek myths we read, heroes also had to beat monsters to prove themselves. It shows that people valued courage."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: finding a pattern","tryThis":"Give a short list of starter patterns to look for (a hero facing a monster, gods who ignore or harm humans, a magical object, a journey or quest) and have students find one scene for each. Provide the frame: 'In Chapter __, ___ happens. In the myth ___, ___ also happens.'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to add a fourth column explaining what fear or value each pattern shows and how the modern setting changes it."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students prepare evidence, then hold a small-group academic discussion on how myths reflect cultural values, tracing fears, values, and patterns and comparing the novel to myths from other cultures.","activities":[{"id":"lia-prepare-evidence","title":"Prepare Evidence and Model a Response","minutes":8,"standards":["SL.6.1.a","RL.6.9","SL.6.6"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"Chapters 1–12, including Ch. 11 (pp. 178–187) and Ch. 12"},{"type":"directions","text":"Review your Patterns Chart. Choose two pieces of evidence: one from The Lightning Thief and one from a myth. Mark the chapter, page, or myth title. Write one sentence explaining what each shows about cultural values."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I will model first. My claim: myths reflect what a culture fears or values. In The Lightning Thief, the monsters appear in ordinary places, like a school or a roadside store, so the danger feels close to home. Taken together with the myths, this suggests people have always told stories about threats they cannot easily see."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Highlight your cause-and-effect words (because, so that) and your citing verbs (shows, suggests, reveals). Display this stem: 'In ___ (chapter or myth title), ___ shows ___. Similarly, in ___, ___. Taken together, this suggests ___ about what people value.'"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using your evidence, how does Chapter 12 show a modern value about the environment or human actions, and how does that differ from the values in a traditional myth?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Chapter 12 shows a modern value because it makes the effect people have on nature seem important and worth worrying about. In the myth we read, nature is controlled by gods and people mostly respond to what the gods want. So the novel adds a modern idea that humans are also responsible for the world."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Which statement best explains how The Lightning Thief connects to traditional myths?","choices":[{"text":"It repeats the same plots as the myths without changing anything.","correct":false,"rationale":"The novel keeps mythic patterns but sets them in the modern world and adds modern values, so it is not a simple copy."},{"text":"It uses mythic characters, monsters, and patterns but places them in a modern setting that reflects modern concerns.","correct":true,"rationale":"Percy meets gods and monsters from myth in modern places, and the story reflects both old and new values."},{"text":"It has no connection to myths because the story is set today.","correct":false,"rationale":"The characters and events come directly from Greek myth, so the connection is central to the book."},{"text":"It shows that all cultures tell myths with exactly the same values.","correct":false,"rationale":"Myths share some patterns, but students are comparing them to see similarities and differences."}]},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Before the discussion, confirm that students have located the Chapter 12 passage in their own copies. Page numbers vary by edition, and the Ch. 11 pages in the Outline are pp. 178–187. Accept any passage that shows the characters' relationship to nature or the effects of human actions."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students prepare precise claims with evidence from the novel and a myth, using comparison and citing language, before they speak.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Find one detail in the novel and one in a myth. Tell your partner using a frame.' Ask: 'What does this detail show about what people fear or value?' Frames: 'In The Lightning Thief (Ch. __), ___ shows ___.' 'In the myth ___, ___.' 'Both stories show ___.' Emerging: 'In the novel, ___. In the myth, ___.' Expanding: 'In Chapter __, ___ shows ___. Similarly, in the myth, ___.' Bridging: 'In Chapter __, ___ shows ___. In contrast, the myth ___. Taken together, they suggest ___.' Students may plan first in their home language, then say the sentence in English.","watchFor":"If students give only a plot summary, then prompt: 'What does this show about what people care about?' If students cite only one text, then prompt: 'Add one detail from the other text.' Success: students state one claim with evidence from the novel and a myth. Emerging: names one detail from each text with a frame. Expanding: explains what each detail shows. Bridging: compares the two details with precise language and explains the shared value."}]},{"id":"lia-discussion-round-one","title":"Group Discussion Round One: Fears, Values, and Patterns","minutes":11,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Small-group Discussion","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"In your group, discuss this question for about 11 minutes: What fears, values, and recurring patterns are emerging in The Lightning Thief so far? Use specific scenes, characters, and events from Chapters 1–12. Remember your roles and norms."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What fears do you see showing up in the story through monsters, gods, or dangerous places? Use a specific scene."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"One fear is losing family. In Chapter 1, Percy's mother is taken in the attack, and in later chapters he risks a lot to save her. In the myths, heroes often go on journeys because someone they love is in danger. It shows that people value loyalty to family."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What patterns repeat across the chapters? How do those patterns match or differ from myths from other cultures?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A pattern is that the hero gets help from friends or magical gifts, like Annabeth's cap or Percy's pen-sword. In myths from other cultures we read, heroes also get help from allies or special objects. I think that shows many cultures value teamwork and that no one succeeds alone."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and listen for evidence with locations, paraphrasing before adding on, and comparisons with a myth. Prompt silent groups with: 'Paraphraser, restate that idea. Connector, link it to a myth.' Keep a quick tally of who has contributed."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: starting or sustaining talk","tryThis":"Give a two-step routine: state a claim ('I noticed that ___.'), then support it ('In Chapter __, ___ shows ___.'). Let the Facilitator ask, 'Who can add evidence?'"},{"situation":"Struggling with: paraphrasing","tryThis":"Provide frames: 'I heard you say ___.' 'In other words, ___.' 'Do I have that right?'"},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask: 'Which pattern in the novel is most modern, and which is most ancient? Defend your choice with two pieces of evidence.'"}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in contributing to a structured discussion, using evidence and paraphrasing peers' ideas.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Use a stem each time you speak.' Ask: 'Which scene shows this fear or value?' Frames: 'I agree with ___ because ___.' 'I heard ___ say ___.' 'Can you point to where the text shows that?' 'One pattern is ___.' Emerging: 'I think ___.' 'In Chapter __, ___ happens.' Expanding: 'I agree with ___ because in Chapter __, ___.' Bridging: 'Building on ___'s idea, Chapter __ shows ___, which is similar to the myth ___.' Allow students to rehearse a sentence with a partner first.","watchFor":"If students agree without reasons, then prompt: 'Add because and a detail.' If students tell personal stories only, then prompt: 'Connect back to a scene.' Success: students speak at least once, cite a scene, and paraphrase a peer. Emerging: speaks once with a frame and names a chapter. Expanding: builds on a peer with a detail. Bridging: builds on peers and connects the novel to a myth using precise language."}]},{"id":"lia-discussion-round-two","title":"Group Discussion Round Two: How Do Myths Reflect Cultural Values?","minutes":11,"standards":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Small-group Discussion","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Rotate roles. Now discuss the essential question: How do myths reflect cultural values? Compare patterns in The Lightning Thief to myths from other cultures. Use evidence from at least two sources and say where it comes from."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How are the values in The Lightning Thief similar to the values in a myth from another culture, and how are they different?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Both the novel and the myth we read value courage and loyalty because the heroes risk themselves to protect others. A difference is that in the novel, Chapter 12 also brings in modern ideas about the environment and what people do to the world. In the old myth, the main focus is the gods' power, not human responsibility."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Taking all of our evidence together, how do myths reflect cultural values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Myths show what a culture fears and admires through monsters and heroes. The novel borrows those patterns but updates them, so the values of today get mixed with ancient ones. This means stories can change as culture changes."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Stop groups at the 10-minute mark and invite the Paraphraser in each group to restate one key idea from their discussion to the class in formal English. Listen for SL.6.1.d (reflecting multiple perspectives) and RL.6.9 (comparison, not just retelling)."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: comparing across texts","tryThis":"Hand students a two-column frame: 'In the novel ___. In the myth ___. Both show ___.' Have them fill in one row before speaking."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask: 'How might a reader from another culture read Percy's quest differently, and what values would they notice?'"}]},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students synthesize across the novel and myths and use comparison language in extended, formal speech.","sayAsk":"Say: 'Compare one thing in the novel to one thing in a myth.' Ask: 'What is the same? What is different? What does that show about values?' Frames: 'Both ___ and ___ show ___.' 'In contrast, ___.' 'This suggests that people value ___.' Emerging: 'The novel and the myth both have ___.' Expanding: 'Both stories show ___, but in the novel ___.' Bridging: 'Although both stories show ___, the novel differs because ___; taken together, they suggest ___.'","watchFor":"If students list differences only, then prompt: 'What value is shared?' If students use informal language, then prompt: 'Say that again in formal English.' Success: students use one comparison phrase and cite both texts. Emerging: names one similarity with a frame. Expanding: names a similarity and a difference. Bridging: explains what the comparison suggests about cultural values."}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect in a Quick Write on how the discussion changed or deepened their thinking about myths and cultural values.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: A New Connection","minutes":5,"standards":["SL.6.1.d","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write two to three sentences in response to the prompt."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one idea from today's discussion that changed or added to your thinking about how myths reflect cultural values? Name the text or scene it came from."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A classmate pointed out that the monsters in The Lightning Thief show up in everyday places, like myths where danger appears in ordinary life. That made me think myths show what a culture fears most. Now I see that Percy's story is like an old myth with modern fears added."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Collect the Quick Writes to check for evidence-based thinking and comparison. Use them to plan the Meaning-Making Huddle on the next Flex Day."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional reading that prepares students for the next chapter of the novel.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch13","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 13","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the summary of Chapter 13 (pp. 197–201). Then read and annotate Chapter 13 of The Lightning Thief (pp. 202–211). As you read, mark one moment that connects to a pattern from today's discussion."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students prepared evidence from Chapters 1–12 of The Lightning Thief and from myths of other cultures, then held two rounds of small-group academic discussion on how myths reflect cultural values. They traced fears, values, and recurring patterns, compared the novel to traditional myths, and practiced formal English with defined group roles.","keyActivities":["Turn and Talk on Chapter 12 and modern values about nature and human actions","Co-constructing roles, norms, and formal English expectations","Patterns Chart comparing the novel to myths from other cultures","Two rounds of small-group discussion on the essential question","Quick Write on a new connection"],"vocabularyTaught":["cultural value","pattern","synthesize","paraphrase","formal English"],"standardsCovered":["SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1.b","SL.6.1.c","SL.6.1.d","SL.6.6","RL.6.9"]}}
